archetype: Mono-black aristocrats-combo: a sacrifice engine that draws while it assembles and closes with one of four rules-verified drain loops — two of them unbounded, and three of them naming neither the commander nor Nest of Scarabs.

role_assignment.default_role: THE QUIET COMBO DECK — control posture, combo clock. Duke's operational test in strategy:whos-the-beatdown is 'who has inevitability? — whoever loses the long game must be the beatdown', and in a fair pod that is you: a commander whose ability reads 'Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature: Put a -1/-1 counter on up to one target creature and draw a card' (cards.json) costs no mana and turns every spare body into a card, and strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock's Commander correction is that 'four-player games trend long, so inevitability compounds — engines are the default winning plan'. But do not confuse the posture with the plan. The plan is assembly. strategy:critical-mass names the shape and its price in one sentence — 'linear strategies give up flexibility in exchange for power', so 'the deck's defense is speed, redundancy, and resilience, not answers' — which is exactly what deck-audit measures: interaction-breadth 2 classes answered against a target of 5, while the redundancy the school asks for is present at every enabler layer (goldfish_metrics.json, 10,000 iterations, seed 42, unassisted / tutor-assisted by turn 10): a drain 82.4% / 94.1%, a free repeatable sacrifice outlet 77.9% / 92.0%, renewable fodder 73.6% / 90.0%, an ignition source 73.1% / 90.0%, engine mana 61.9% / 85.1%, a tutor 60.6%. The commander lands on turn 4 in 7,220 of 10,000 games, mean 4.294, 91.1% by turn 6; keep-first-seven is 0.818 at a mean 0.216 mulligans, and the turn-3 land drop hits 0.919. So you sit under the radar and you look like a value deck — strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection is blunt that this is a playbook read in reverse: 'combo decks look non-threatening while advancing in secret, which is exactly why experienced tables hit the quiet ramp player', so expect your own 'I haven't done anything' to be discounted. Role stays seat-relative (strategy:whos-the-beatdown, Commander correction): control against fair midrange, and the beatdown against any deck whose lock or clock arrives before your assembly (strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial).
role_assignment.pivot_trigger: ONE ASSEMBLY IS THE TABLE, NOT A SEAT — and that is the whole pivot. All four checker-passed kills take four opponents from 40 to 0 simultaneously: stack 009 (pass) has 40 drain events per seat with one already resolved, so '39 further iterations take all four opponents to 0 at once'; stack 011 (pass) is the same arithmetic and 'you end at 80 life'; stack 012 (pass) says 'Drain #40 takes all four opponents from 1 to 0 simultaneously -- Not a draw -- you win'; stack 010 (pass) needs 39 further activations against a 59-card library, so 'All four opponents reach 0 together and leave the game; you are still in it, so you win (104.2a)'. The go decision therefore stops being body arithmetic and becomes a two-part check. (1) CONFIGURATION: is what you hold one of the four verified shapes — Gravecrawler plus a sacrifice-to-mana plus a second Zombie plus an each-opponent drain (009, 011); Exquisite Blood plus a body reading 'Whenever you gain life, each opponent loses 1 life' (012); Mikaeus plus the commander plus a non-Human body plus a drain (010)? (2) INTERACTION: strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window sets the bar the table applies to you — 'does this card win the game if it resolves' — and instructs you to 'assume every held answer appears the moment you present lethal, and count the table's open mana before committing'. Two of these attempts are unusually cheap to make, which matters because the same section says to 'prefer win attempts that leave a rebuilt position if they fail': 009 is life-neutral per iteration (floor 39, refunded to 40) and 011 pays nothing at all and gains 1 per iteration. Sequence the scariest piece last so the deflection budget lasts to the turn you take it; strategy:tempo.sequencing's Commander correction — commit 'at the end step before your own turn so the table's chances to respond are spent' — is the right default for deploying the drain, because the drain is the piece that reveals the plan. The bounded arithmetic still governs the median board and only the median board: with the commander and Nest of Scarabs the engine terminates by body exhaustion at 5 to 8 activations (stacks 002 and 005, both pass), which is a value ceiling, not a kill.

engines.engine: THE SELF-FUNDING RECURSION LOOP — the deck's Plan A and the only slot in it with no substitute. Gravecrawler's own ability modifies the zone it can be cast from, so with any other Zombie on board it recasts itself every iteration; pair it with something that turns a sacrifice into mana and with an each-opponent drain and the loop pays for its own next cast. Two verified configurations: Warren Soultrader (Treasure) and Phyrexian Altar ({B} directly).
engines.evidence: verified stack 009 ('each activation's Treasure exactly funds the next cast. The loop is self-funding and unbounded'); verified stack 011 ('The board returns to an identical state, so the loop is unbounded'); goldfish_metrics.json 0.165 unassisted / 0.665 assisted by turn 10, mean draw turn 3.764

engines.engine: THE SHARED PAYOFF — 'Whenever a creature you control dies, each opponent loses 1 life and you gain 1 life' (cards.json) is the drain three of the four verified kills route through (009, 010, 011), which makes it the deck's single most load-bearing noncreature permanent. Zulaport Cutthroat and Ayara, First of Locthwain are the declared substitutes; The Meathook Massacre, Marauding Blight-Priest and Starscape Cleric widen the class to nine cards, measured at 82.4% by turn 10.
engines.evidence: verified stacks 009, 010, 011; goldfish_metrics.json Bastion 0.167 / 0.662, the drain class 0.824 / 0.941

engines.engine: THE MANDATORY TWO-CARD LOOP — the only kill that needs no sacrifice outlet inside the loop and no recursion. 'Whenever an opponent loses life, you gain that much life' against a body reading 'Whenever you gain life, each opponent loses 1 life' alternates one drain per cycle; the checker settled that this is a win and not the CR 104.4b draw case, because every iteration lowers every opponent's life. Three bodies carry that text — South Wind Avatar, Marauding Blight-Priest, Starscape Cleric.
engines.evidence: verified stack 012 ('the sequence is not one that could be repeated indefinitely (732.1b) and there is a way to stop (104.4b)'); combo_details bracket-3 lines Exquisite Blood + Marauding Blight-Priest and + Starscape Cleric; goldfish 0.069 / 0.425 by turn 10, mean turn 5.301 — the fastest of the four

engines.engine: THE LIBRARY-BOUNDED ANNIHILATION LOOP — the one kill that uses the commander, and the one that is finite. The commander's -1/-1 counter annihilates undying's +1/+1 and re-arms the body; the loop's own mandatory draw is what ends it. 39 further activations are needed against 59 the library permits, so the margin is 20 clean and at most 25 if the free sacrifice outlet is saved as a finisher.
engines.evidence: verified stack 010 ('a library-bounded loop, not an infinite combo ... it holds with 20 activations of margin (20-25 depending on finisher Seer sacrifices)')

engines.engine: THE MEDIAN ENGINE — a mana-free, instant-speed sacrifice outlet stapled to a draw engine, and one kill's middle. Its ability costs no mana at all, which is the deck's strongest property under a tax or a lock. Pilot it as the draw engine it is, not as the plan: three of four verified kills never name it.
engines.evidence: oracle text (cards.json: 'Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature: Put a -1/-1 counter on up to one target creature and draw a card'); verified stack 010 uses him; verified stacks 009, 011, 012 do not

engines.engine: THE FODDER CONVERTER — 'Whenever you put one or more -1/-1 counters on a creature, create that many 1/1 black Insect creature tokens' turns the commander's removal mode into bodies, and its arithmetic is settled: the number of creatures you touch sets the number of triggers, and the counters on each of those creatures set that trigger's 'that many'. One proliferate across three counter-bearing creatures makes three Insects, not four and not six. It feeds the median board; it is not on the critical path of any verified kill.
engines.evidence: verified stack 013 ('the Nest's output has two independent inputs'; three triggers, three tokens); verified stacks 002, 003, 004, 005 bound the commander-plus-Nest engine at 5 to 8 activations by body exhaustion

engines.engine: ENGINE MANA — the class that converts a creature death into castable black and makes the recursion loops self-funding. Five cards: Phyrexian Altar, Pitiless Plunderer, Phyrexian Tower, Black Market Connections, Warren Soultrader. Note the distinction the audit draws: most of the 11 'ramp' copies are engine mana rather than acceleration, and the fast-mana class is only three cards.
engines.evidence: goldfish_metrics.json engine mana 0.619 / 0.851 by turn 10 versus fast mana 0.427 / 0.775; verified stack 011 (Phyrexian Altar's ability 'is a mana ability, so it never used the stack (605.3b)')

engines.engine: THE ASYMMETRY CONVERTER — 'Whenever a creature you control dies, each other player sacrifices a creature of their choice' takes the identical activations that feed a drain and turns them into table-wide edicts, which is the shape strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry asks for: 'Your cards should do something to all three seats or win the game.' It is also the deck's only repeatable answer to a creature it cannot target.
engines.evidence: oracle text (cards.json); card_roles.json files it removal:edict, the deck's only copy of that role

engines.engine: THE DRAW LAYER, priced in life — with Black Market Connections, Skullclamp, Castle Locthwain, Plumb the Forbidden, Ayara and the commander himself. card_roles.json counts only 5 card-advantage copies, which reads UNDER the audit's target of 10 and understates the deck: the audit's own probe note names five more the taxonomy files elsewhere. strategy:card-advantage's Commander correction is the reason the axis is not a finding here — 'engines that out-draw three players are the format's defining advantage'.
engines.evidence: deck-audit card-advantage 5 copies with a probe note naming Ayara, Black Market Connections, Castle Locthwain, Plumb the Forbidden and Yawgmoth; verified stack 010 counts the commander's draw explicitly, capping that loop at 59 activations

engines.engine: THE BREADTH SLOT — 'Destroy target creature or enchantment an opponent controls' is the deck's answer to a noncreature permanent, and it is one card. strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite puts 'breadth before depth: three opponents mean every permanent type appears, so cover the classes — creature, artifact, enchantment, graveyard, land — before doubling any', and deck-audit reads 2 classes answered against a target of 5 (Bojuka Bog exiles a graveyard and is filed land:tapped, so the heuristic's count is a floor). Every verified kill is a small pile of permanents on the battlefield in a deck that can answer almost none.
engines.evidence: oracle text (cards.json); deck-audit interaction-breadth 2 classes vs target 5, with the note that artifact, graveyard and land show no detected answer; goldfish_metrics.json 0.173 unassisted / 0.669 assisted by turn 10

candidate_missing_lines.title: The Meathook Massacre as a fourth substitute drain in the recursion loops
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: Oracle text: 'Whenever a creature you control dies, each opponent loses 1 life' is the same trigger condition and the same each-opponent reach that stack 011 verified on Bastion of Remembrance. If it substitutes, the drain slot of both unbounded recursion kills widens from three cards to four and the kill becomes robust to enchantment removal aimed at Bastion. goldfish_targets.json already counts it in the nine-card drain class but not in KILL A or KILL B's any_of.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Exquisite Blood plus Marauding Blight-Priest or Starscape Cleric — the same loop without the Avatar
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: Both read 'Whenever you gain life, each opponent loses 1 life' verbatim, the identical text stack 012 resolved on South Wind Avatar's second ability, and combo_details carries both as bracket-3 two-card infinites. The unresolved half is the IGNITION: 012's board starts the loop from the Avatar's own dies-trigger lifegain, and neither Blight-Priest nor Starscape Cleric gains life by itself, so the line needs an external first lifegain event that the verified board did not require.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Whether a single-target drain still kills a pod once the loop is unbounded
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: combo_details carries this as a bracket-1 infinite producing 'Infinite lifeloss'. Stack 004 (pass) measured Blood Artist at 8 pod life against Zulaport Cutthroat's 28 on the identical board — but that board is the commander-plus-Nest engine, which terminates by body exhaustion, so the penalty there is a division of a FINITE trigger count. On an unbounded loop the iteration count is the pilot's choice and the penalty may be only a matter of iterations, seat by seat rather than all at once. Nothing verified settles it, and the deckbuilding consequence (prefer each-opponent text, do not cut on the 8-versus-28 figure) hangs on the answer.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Mikaeus plus a free sacrifice outlet, without the commander
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: combo_details carries seven such two-card records (Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Woe Strider, Yahenni, Blasting Station, Phyrexian Altar, Ashnod's Altar), each tagged 'Infinite death triggers'. Stack 010 (pass) resolved the version WITH the commander and found the commander's -1/-1 counter is what annihilates undying's +1/+1 and re-arms the body — and even then the loop is finite. On plain oracle reading a body that returns with a +1/+1 counter does not undie a second time, so the bare two-card records are the deck's largest block of unverified containment and the most likely to be refuted. Eight of the eleven two-card infinites in bracket_report.json belong to this family.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Gravecrawler plus Phyrexian Altar as a literal two-card infinite
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: This is the deck's most popular containment record (60,592) and bracket_report.json cites it as the example two-card infinite forcing the floor. Stack 011 (pass) verified the loop on a four-card board — the Altar, Carrion Feeder as the Zombie satisfying Gravecrawler's graveyard-cast condition, and Bastion as the drain. Gravecrawler's own text requires 'you control a Zombie', so the bare pair appears to be short a piece; whether any two-card configuration exists is unresolved, and the bracket driver rests on the record rather than on a resolution.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Black Sun's Zenith at X greater than 1 into Nest of Scarabs
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: Stack 013 (pass) explicitly declines to resolve it and names it as the case its reading would scale differently: 'Put X -1/-1 counters on each creature' places X counters per creature in one event, so applying 013's reading to three of your creatures at X=3 would give three triggers of three tokens each. 013 states that arithmetic as a consequence of its own reading and NOT as resolved. It matters for a sweeper slot that is the only one of the deck's scalable wipes that places counters at all.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Pitiless Plunderer plus Ashnod's Altar plus Reassembling Skeleton — infinite mana with no drain attached
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: combo_details rates this at 52,227 popularity producing 'Infinite colorless mana' and 'Infinite death triggers'. Every piece is in the 99 and the Skeleton returns itself for {1}{B}, so the mana half is plausible on oracle reading; the death-trigger half would make it a fifth kill the moment any of the nine drains is on board. It is not counted as a kill anywhere and should not be until it is resolved.

matchup_frames.vs_sweeper_control: A sweeper is a payoff, not a loss — and the danger is aimed one permanent type higher. Nine cards read some form of 'a creature you control dies, each opponent loses life', so a wrath that empties your board pays you for every body it takes, and 28 creatures plus Reassembling Skeleton and Gravecrawler make you the cheapest rebuilder at the table. strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math's Commander correction is the right default anyway — 'assume the wrath — over a four-player game one is near-certain — so deploy in waves, hold a rebuild package, and when possible let another player's board be the reason it gets cast'. The real exposure is that every verified kill is a pile of PERMANENTS and the loops route through noncreature ones: Bastion of Remembrance in three of the four, Exquisite Blood and Phyrexian Altar in the others. The deck's protection effects all protect a creature, so the enchantment that closes the game cannot be saved, and the answer to a resolved enchantment or artifact aimed at you is one card (Feed the Swarm, 0.173 unassisted / 0.669 assisted by turn 10). strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite's 'breadth before depth' names this precisely; strategy:resource-hedging is the posture — 'hedge from ahead, gamble from behind' — so hold the drain in hand until the turn it converts, and lead with the piece the table is least likely to spend an answer on.
matchup_frames.vs_stax: This is the matchup the deck is quietly built for, and the reason is verified rather than argued: three of the four kills need essentially no external mana once assembled. Stack 009's Treasure 'exactly funds the next cast', stack 011's Phyrexian Altar 'is a mana ability, so it never used the stack' and refunds its own {B} each iteration, and stack 012's loop is mandatory and spends nothing. The commander's activated ability costs no mana at all. strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial forces the role — 'you rarely own the long game under an assembling lock, so you are the beatdown, racing the lock's completion' — and gives the discipline: 'Name your outs early — the removal or velocity that breaks the piece that beats YOU, not the scariest piece'. Under a tax, recount your hand rather than your board: a Sphere effect halves a two-spell turn but does nothing to a loop that is already running. The pieces that genuinely beat you are graveyard hate (BOTH unbounded kills cast Gravecrawler out of the graveyard, once per iteration) and a noncreature lock permanent you cannot destroy — and that second class is the one the deck answers with one card.
matchup_frames.vs_aggro: You are the control deck and you should stop apologising for the sweepers. Four scalable wipes (Black Sun's Zenith, Toxic Deluge, The Meathook Massacre, Soul Snuffers), 13 interaction copies, Grave Pact converting your own engine into table-wide edicts, and 28 bodies to chump or eat make this the deck's most comfortable seat; deck-audit reads sweepers OVER against a 1-3 target while strategy:deckbuilding.ratios' Command Zone template says 3-4, so four is the top of the band, not an excess. Life is not the pressure point it looks like: stack 011 ends the pilot at 80 life and stack 012 gains 40, while the commander costs 1 per activation and Necropotence 1 per card. strategy:life-as-resource is the frame — 'its points appreciate as they dwindle, so early points are cheap and late points are priceless' — so spend freely on cards early and switch to defending 'one turn before it matters, not one after'. strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy sets the bar for the spot removal: 'ends the game or ends my deck's function', not 'looks scary', and point the commander's -1/-1 counters at opponents' small creatures whenever a legal target exists, because on the bounded board an opposing 2-toughness creature EXTENDS the engine by two activations rather than bounding it (stacks 002 and 003, both pass).
matchup_frames.vs_combo: The worst seat, because the deck cannot interact on the stack at all and its own kill needs a board. Mono-black's answer set stops at permanents: Deadly Rollick is free with a commander out, Snuff Out is free with a Swamp, and neither touches a spell. strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy's countervailing clause is the operative one — 'held answers rot — against combo, or lethal already on board, the last profitable moment is now' — so spend removal on the enabler the moment it lands rather than at the last profitable moment, and use strategy:critical-mass in reverse: 'play against one by denying the threshold before it snowballs: hit enablers, not payoffs'. Where you can win the race is speed of assembly at instant speed: stack 012's verified board ignites the loop from a free sacrifice outlet's activated ability, so the kill does not need a sorcery-speed step once the two permanents are down (whether the whole assembly can be completed on another player's turn is not verified and should not be claimed). strategy:resource-hedging.playing-to-outs is the posture when you are behind their clock — 'identify the card or event that saves you and play as if it's coming' — which here means committing to the shape you can complete rather than the one you would prefer.
matchup_frames.vs_graveyard_hate: Named separately because it is the archetype's primary hoser and it is asymmetric across this deck's four kills. Both unbounded kills cast Gravecrawler from the graveyard every iteration (stacks 009 and 011), so a Rest in Peace effect blanks the deck's entire unbounded half outright — but stack 012's loop touches no graveyard at all, and stack 010's runs on undying returns from the battlefield, so what a hate piece leaves you is exactly the two bounded kills. The deck's redundancy is therefore real but uneven, and the correct read under hate is to abandon the recursion shape entirely and tutor for Exquisite Blood plus a lifegain-drain body, which is also the fastest of the four (mean draw turn 5.301). strategy:resource-hedging.playing-to-outs: 'know what you can't beat and stop paying for it'.

distribution_notes: 36 lands and 42 mana sources against strategy:deckbuilding.ratios' 36-38 band, 3 taplands, and B at 34 land sources plus 8 nonland against a 36-source target for 75 pips across 55 cards (deck-facts, mana_analysis.json) — on-curve 0.882 on lands alone, 0.955 counting rocks and dorks. The curve is 14 / 17 / 18 / 11 / 2 / 2 from one to six, modal 3 against strategy:deckbuilding.curve's format-modal 2, with nothing above six; the verified kills are cheap enough that this reads as slack at the top rather than a problem — 009's three pieces cost {2}{B}, {B} and {2}{B}. Role coverage is 97.5%, with only Plumb the Forbidden and Supernatural Stamina unclassified; the histogram's shape is the archetype's — threat:body 28, sac-cost 12, wincon:drain 12, value:etb 12, sac-outlet 9, against removal totalling 17 across five role classes and tutor:unrestricted 5. Three counts deserve to be read as floors rather than verdicts, per deck-audit's own probe notes: card-advantage reads 5 while the oracle text shows the function on six more cards, protection reads 3 while Supernatural Stamina and Malakir Rebirth are filed elsewhere, and interaction-breadth reads 2 because the detector is an oracle-text heuristic. Only the last is a real finding. On the combo layer: 32 lines are fully contained and 11 are two-card infinites, and deck-facts is unambiguous that 'None is verified: a line is fact only once a stack artifact carries checker.verdict == pass' — the verified count is four, and containment is a shortlist, not evidence. The synergy graph places 71 of the deck's cards and finds 57 intra-deck edges, which is a global top-10 shortlist and cannot price fit inside this list. One reading note for anyone building on the stack set: eleven of the thirteen passing stacks resolve boards drawn entirely from the 99, and stacks 001 and 007 resolve a Blowfly Infestation board — they are rules findings about how Nest of Scarabs and a creation-metered drain behave, not lines this list can present.
overall_assessment: This is a combo deck that wears a value engine's clothes, and the evidence for that is four checker-passed kills rather than a containment count. Two are unbounded — stacks 009 and 011 each take a four-opponent pod from 40 to 0 with the loop's own resources, and 011 leaves the pilot at 80 life having paid nothing. The other two are lethal and bounded, by different mechanisms. Stack 012's loop is mandatory but it is not the draw case: the checker's own words are that 'the sequence is not one that could be repeated indefinitely (732.1b) and there is a way to stop (104.4b)' — it is lethal precisely because it ends, drain #40 taking all four opponents from 1 to 0 at one state-based-action check. Stack 010 is bounded by your own library instead, lethal with 20 to 25 activations of margin against a 59-card library. Keep that distinction rather than flattening it: an unbounded loop is a decision you make once, a bounded one is arithmetic you have to count. Three of the four need neither the commander nor Nest of Scarabs — goldfish_targets.json sets `commander: true` on KILL D alone, Nest of Scarabs appears in no kill's `need` groups at all, and stack 012 puts it off the battlefield by assumption. Read that carefully, because it is the whole strategic shape of the deck: the one kill that needs the commander (stack 010) is also the one kill bounded by your own library, and both unbounded lines (009 and 011) are lines he is not in. All four end a four-opponent pod outright; three of them do it without him. That inverts the archetype's best-known failure mode: deck_recon.json (as_of 2026-08-03) records fetched community guidance that removal on Yawgmoth stops these decks outright, and for THIS list it does not. strategy:multiplayer.commander-insurance is the section that prices the consequence — 'how critical is the commander to the plan, and what removal this table actually runs' — and at three kills out of four the honest answer here is not 'less critical' but 'not critical', which by that section's own racing alternative means skip the insurance, pay the recast tax, rebuild. Do not hold up mana for him and do not mulligan toward him; he is a draw engine, a redundant free outlet and a removal magnet you should be pleased to trade. What the deck is playing for, then, is assembly, and strategy:critical-mass is the school: 'a linear deck is entirely focused on one goal or theme', its defense is 'speed, redundancy, and resilience, not answers', and its Commander correction is exactly this list's shape — 'the linear deck needs redundancy that shrugs off three answers, or a deflection posture that keeps them unspent'. The redundancy is measured and it is good at every layer except the kill itself: a drain 82.4%, a free sacrifice outlet 77.9%, fodder 73.6%, an ignition source 73.1%, engine mana 61.9% by turn 10 unassisted, rising to roughly 90% with a tutor (goldfish_metrics.json, 10,000 iterations, seed 42). The kills are where the thinness lives, and the numbers are small on purpose: KILL A 1.1% / 18.0%, KILL B 0.5% / 12.3%, KILL C 6.9% / 42.5%, KILL D 4.6% / 33.7% unassisted / tutor-assisted by turn 10. Seven declared components rest on a single named card, and a named card is 7.1% of an opening seven — that is the arithmetic of singleton (strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors), not a defect in the list. Do not reach for a composite, because there is no honest one. goldfish_targets.json states the constraint in its own words: `goldfish._target_met` counts each need group independently, so the schema is an AND of ORs and 'genuinely cannot express an OR of ANDs; a deck with four independent kills therefore has no single assembled_rate here, and any figure presented as one is wrong. Quote the per-kill rates.' Nor can you manufacture the union out of the four yourself: these kills are independent as routes and overlapping as cards — Gravecrawler sits in two of them and the same three-card drain class in three — so adding the rates double-counts, and multiplying them as independent events is wrong in the other direction. Four measurements are what the simulation supports, and four measurements is what you quote. The honest statement is the one strategy:deckbuilding.threat-density asks for: count how many of the 99 produce the win — four independent verified lines, sharing a drain slot and a recursive body, which is the section's own reconciliation of Eisenherz's two-combo cap ('Layering reconciles them: overlap pieces, so five cards support four combos') and its median-build standard ('the ceiling build runs one spectacular finisher and loses when it's answered; the median runs three cheap ones and closes from any board'). This is a median build with four closers, and it should be piloted as one. What binds is not conversion and not bodies; it is breadth. Every verified kill is a small pile of permanents sitting on the battlefield in a deck that answers two of the five permanent classes strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite asks you to cover, with exactly one card that destroys a noncreature permanent an opponent controls. That is the linear deck's stated price — 'interaction slots are the price of the engine' — and it is the axis on which this list actually loses: not to a wrath, which pays it, but to a resolved artifact or enchantment it cannot remove, or to graveyard hate that blanks the recursion shape while leaving the Exquisite Blood shape live. The bracket conversation follows from the same evidence and is now easy to have straight: bracket_report.json's floor is 4, forced independently by four Game Changers and by eleven two-card infinite records, and strategy:deckbuilding.power-level's standard — 'Contents give a floor, never a verdict', Bracket 4 being 'lethal, consistent, and fast', at least four turns — is met by the verified lines rather than argued from containment. Say it plainly at Rule 0: four rules-verified kills, two of them unbounded, each of which ends all four opponents simultaneously. Then play the deck that description implies. Deploy the outlet and the fodder early and cheaply, use the commander to draw for three or four turns before you use him for anything else, keep the drain in hand until the turn it converts, present the assembly at the end step before your own turn so the table's answers are spent (strategy:tempo.sequencing), and go when the configuration is one of the four and the table's open mana is counted — because one assembly is no longer a seat. It is the table.
gaps: STANDS, and it is still the largest hole. No aristocrats / sacrifice-loop section exists anywhere in the corpus. The doc has nothing on the outlet / fodder / payoff triad, which is this deck's entire architecture; a query for 'sacrifice outlet aristocrats engine' tops out at 0.270 against strategy:mulligans.engine-hands, and no heading names any of the three functions. It generalises to every Blood Artist, token-sacrifice and Aristocrats deck in the format.

CLOSED FOR THIS DECK BY EVIDENCE, STANDS IN THE DOC, AND IS NOW SHARPER. 'What bounds an iterative engine' is answered here line by line rather than by theory: stack 010 is bounded by the LIBRARY (59 permitted against 39 needed, margin 20-25), stacks 002 and 005 are bounded by BODIES (5 and 8 activations, ended by body exhaustion), and stacks 009, 011 and 012 are bounded by nothing at all — they terminate only because the payoff is finite, at 40 drain events per seat. The doc still has no vocabulary for the distinction the checker had to draw with CR 732.1b: a loop that is unbounded IN THE RULES SENSE versus a loop that terminates because the thing it is producing runs out. strategy:critical-mass.storm-math covers velocity and the go decision and never asks which resource runs out first.

STANDS, DEMOTED. No theory of trigger SURFACE — creation-side versus death-side payoffs. Stack 008 (pass) establishes that one commander activation paid with a token produces TWO triggers on a drain reading 'whenever you create or sacrifice a token' and one on a death-metered drain, because the sacrifice is an activation cost paid while the ability is already on the stack. The doc has no section in which that distinction, or 'a bigger body is a liability on a loop that needs something to die', is even expressible. It governs the median board rather than the kills, so it is a smaller hole than the corpus's other ones.

STANDS, SHARPENED. strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors counts copies of an effect class and has no notion that a RECURSIVE copy is worth more than a one-shot one. Gravecrawler is one card at 16.5% of openers by that section's arithmetic, and it is also the reason stacks 009 and 011 are unbounded at all — the loop exists because the card recasts itself. Reassembling Skeleton is priced identically to a body that dies once. Renewability belongs in that section's hypergeometric.

STANDS, AND IS NOW PARTLY ANSWERABLE FROM EVIDENCE. Nothing in the doc treats mana-free or self-funding lines as a class. The commander's ability costs no mana; stack 009's loop funds its own next cast from a Treasure; stack 011's Phyrexian Altar refunds its own {B} and never uses the stack; stack 012 spends nothing. That is this deck's strongest property against taxes and locks and it is verified, but strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial's advice stops at 'recount your hand under the tax' and has no term for a kill that runs on zero external mana.

STANDS FOR THE CORPUS, ANSWERED FOR THIS DECK. Life as ENGINE FUEL rather than as a buffer: strategy:life-as-resource treats life as currency spent on cards and turns. Here the loops' life ledgers are verified and favourable — stack 011 is +1 per iteration and ends at 80, stack 012 ends at 80, stack 009 is net 0 with a floor of 39 — against per-activation costs on the commander, Necropotence, Bitterblossom and Feed the Swarm. The break-even reasoning has no home in the doc, but this deck no longer needs it to make a decision.

CLOSED FOR THIS DECK. How to discuss a bracket floor when the lines forcing it are unverified is no longer this list's problem: four kills are checker-passed and the floor is independently forced by four Game Changers. The general guidance gap remains — bracket_report.json's own note calls brackets 'a conversation, not a calculator' and strategy:deckbuilding.power-level.barometers gives no procedure for a Rule 0 conversation whose combo content is a containment record rather than a resolution — but it no longer binds here.

STANDS, AND THE ARTIFACTS CANNOT ANSWER IT EITHER. The doc has no theory for reading several partially-overlapping win conditions as one probability, and neither does the simulator: goldfish_targets.json is an AND of ORs, so each of the four kills carries its own rate and their union has no expression at all — which is why this frame quotes KILL A through KILL D separately and offers no aggregate. The nearest sections are the wrong shape. strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors does the hypergeometric for copies of ONE effect class ('5 copies is 31% of openers, 7 is 41% ... 10 is 54%'), and strategy:combat-math.probability supplies the method for a single will-I-have-it-by-turn-X question — 'count successes in the deck and cards seen, read the cumulative probability'. Neither says what to do with four multi-card conjunctions that share pieces and are therefore correlated. The honest alternative — name the count of independent lines, quote each line's rate, decline to invent a fifth number — is a discipline this deck has to supply for itself.

NEW. Nothing on how to pilot a deck whose commander is NOT on the critical path, in a format built around commanders. strategy:multiplayer.commander-insurance answers 'how much protection does the engine's hub deserve' and the answer here is 'none, he is not the hub' — but the section has no guidance for deliberately offering the commander as a lightning rod while the actual kill assembles elsewhere, which is the concrete deflection play this list wants and which strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection describes only in the abstract.

NEW. No section on ANSWER-CLASS COVERAGE as a loss condition rather than a deckbuilding count. strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite lists the five permanent classes and says to cover them before doubling; it does not discuss what it means to be a combo deck whose own kill is a pile of permanents while holding one answer to a noncreature permanent. The asymmetry — your kill is answerable by classes you cannot answer back — is this deck's binding axis and the corpus can only express half of it.
